intro: PowerPoint for instructional designers on Mac mostly comes down to slide masters, reusable templates and quick storyboards. Set those up once, and every course slide inherits your fonts, colors and layouts. This guide covers the Mac menu paths, the places where long courses strain the format, and where Lazur can help.

blocks.text: Why PowerPoint is still the default tool for course design on Mac

Plenty of instructional designers on Mac still open PowerPoint first. The reasons are practical. Stakeholders can read slides without a special login. Subject matter experts know how to leave comments on a deck. And the file travels well through email and shared drives.

The tool was built for presentations, though, not for course design. That gap shows up in a few places: master templates, storyboards for long courses, and version control. You can work around all of them. You just need to know where the friction sits before a project starts.

Microsoft's Mac help hub covers PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 for Mac, PowerPoint 2024 for Mac and PowerPoint 2021 for Mac. Check which one you run before you follow any steps. Menu names and button locations can differ between them, so a step that works in one may not match another.
Set up slide masters once so fonts and colors stop drifting

The slide master is the most useful feature for course work. It stores your fonts, colors, logo and layouts. Every slide built from it inherits those settings. Change the master, and the whole course updates in one pass.

To open it on Mac, go to View > Slide Master. The thumbnail pane shows a master slide at the top, with layouts listed beneath it. Click a layout to change its placeholders. Click the master to change the theme fonts and colors. These are the steps most designers follow:

items: Open View > Slide Master. The Slide Master tab appears in the ribbon.
Select the top master slide and set the title and body fonts from the Slide Master tab.
Keep the layouts you use most, such as title, text with image, and knowledge check.
Use Insert Layout in the Slide Master tab only for patterns your course really needs.
Select Close Master View when you finish. Your normal slides keep working.

blocks.text: The most common mistake is typing over a placeholder on a regular slide. Once you type into a text box, that box stops following the master. Fix the problem in the layout instead, then reset the slide so it picks up the layout again.
Build a reusable template your team can open from a menu

After the master works, save it as a template. Choose File > Save As, then pick PowerPoint Template (.potx) from the format menu. Press ⇧⌘S if you prefer the keyboard. Name the file for the course type rather than the date, so the team can find it again.

Microsoft's own template article walks through the steps on Windows. Its linked Mac article returned a 404 when checked, so official Mac steps are thin right now. Use the Mac path in this guide, then test it on one file before you roll a template out to a whole team.
Open the template through File > New from Template. Look for your saved file under the personal tab in the template gallery. Tab names can shift between versions, so confirm them on your copy.

Where you keep the file matters too. A shared drive works for a small team. A synced team folder works better, because a copy saved on one laptop goes stale fast, and people start building from the wrong version.

blocks.title: Test before you share
blocks.text: Open the template, add a test slide from every layout, and export a PDF. Catch broken placeholders and odd fonts before a subject expert ever receives the file.
Organization templates and what your Microsoft 365 plan allows

If your company hands out an official template, the license matters. Microsoft says organization templates require a Microsoft 365 E3 or E5 plan. On Mac, you open them from New or File > New from Template, then double-click the template in the folder.

Ask your IT team whether your plan qualifies before you build a course around an organization template. If it does not, your personal .potx file is the fallback. It works without any plan change, and you control its layouts.
Storyboard a course in slides without losing the thread

A storyboard in PowerPoint is one slide per screen. Each slide holds the on-screen text, the narration and the interaction. It is quick to draw and easy for a reviewer to read on any device. That speed is why many designers start here.

rows: One sentence the learner can act on
Spot a phishing email before clicking
The words that appear, kept short
Hover over the link to see where it goes
What the learner does, and the feedback
Click the suspicious link and see the warning
Image, icon or video to source
blocks.caption: One storyboard row per slide keeps reviews fast.

blocks.text: Keep one slide per screen, not one slide per topic. A slide per screen makes the next click obvious to a reviewer. It also shows timing when you read the deck aloud, which catches narration that runs too long.

Put the narration script in the speaker notes. On Mac, open View > Notes, then type under each slide. The script travels with the file, and it stays attached to the slide when someone moves it in the deck.
Where PowerPoint gets cumbersome for long, text-heavy courses

PowerPoint works well for short modules. It gets heavy when a course runs long and text-heavy. An iSpring guide on eLearning storyboards says the format can get 'cumbersome for very long, text-heavy courses.' Many designers hit that wall around the second or third module of a big project.

The same guide lists limited version control as a con, and it rates PowerPoint's co-authoring as basic. Two people editing one deck can overwrite each other's slides. Name each saved version with a date and a reviewer's initials, so you can always roll back.
These workarounds help when the course grows:

items: Split long courses into one file per module, then combine them for export.
Keep the master in one template file, and copy it into each module rather than editing each one.
Store module files in a shared folder that keeps version history.
Export a PDF for reviewers who only comment. Collect every comment in one document.

blocks.text: Designer ideas and AI layouts on Mac: what to check first

Designer, which Microsoft's help calls Design Ideas, suggests layouts for a slide. It needs a Microsoft 365 subscription. Microsoft lists PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 for Mac in the feature's Applies To list, so it should appear on your Mac. Check the Design tab on your copy before you plan around it.

The catch is templates. Microsoft says not all custom templates are compatible with Design Suggestions. Even with a compatible template, suggestions cannot cover every slide. Test it on your course template before you depend on it for a deadline.

For instructional design, treat layout suggestions as drafts. Check that text stays readable, contrast holds up, and the slide still follows your master. A suggested layout that breaks the master is a bad trade, even if it looks sharp.
What the ATD 2025 survey does and does not tell you

A 2025 survey from ATD Research gives the most useful numbers in this area. It covered 232 talent development professionals, and the report went out on August 4, 2025. Most of the figures below come from that one report.

Read those numbers carefully. The survey measures AI tools, not PowerPoint. It does not say how much time PowerPoint costs an instructional designer on Mac. I found no survey that measures that, so any claim about PowerPoint time would be a guess.

Hardman's 2024 State of Instructional Design survey, with almost 500 respondents, reports an average project cost split of 37.7% for development and implementation. That is a share of cost, not time. Use it to understand where budgets go, not to judge a tool.

The fair takeaway is narrow. AI tools are common in this work. In the ATD survey, 37% said they greatly reduced course design time, and 70% said they improve design quality. Your own timing on your own projects will tell you more than any industry average.
Ask Lazur for the Mac steps you keep forgetting

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a command lives, and it draws a circle and a label around that spot.

This fits the slide master problem well. Ask where the slide master is in this PowerPoint, and Lazur points at View > Slide Master. Ask it to walk you through adding a layout, and it guides one click at a time, waiting for each click before it moves on.
Lazur does not click for you. It does not edit your files or operate other apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for PowerPoint. You keep the mouse and every decision about the slides.

For text, hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. That covers alt text, speaker notes and storyboard narration. Lazur can also draft a storyboard row from a learning goal, and you edit it before it goes anywhere.
Right-click menu and Presenter View changes coming to PowerPoint for Mac

Microsoft is changing the slide right-click menu on Mac. Message Center item MC1492164 says Zoom leaves the slide and thumbnail menus because few people use it. Layout and Reset Slide join both menus. Cut and Copy leave the slide menu but stay on the thumbnail menu and the ribbon.

The change rolls out worldwide beginning in early October 2026, and it should be complete by mid-October. It is on by default, with no admin controls. If your team has right-click habits, update your quick reference before the change lands.

A redesigned Presenter View for Mac is also in development. Microsoft's roadmap estimates general availability for November 2026. Roadmap dates are estimates and can move, so check release notes before you plan a live course around the new view.

blocks.title: Dates are targets
blocks.text: Treat the November 2026 Presenter View date as an estimate. Confirm it in Microsoft's own release notes before you change a live session.
Mistakes that break course templates on Mac

items: Typing over placeholders on regular slides instead of editing the layout. The text stops following the master.
Saving the template as a regular .pptx and then overwriting it. Save templates as .potx, and keep the master file separate.
Building the template in PowerPoint for the web. Microsoft says the web version cannot create templates.
Pasting from Word or a browser. Pasted text carries its own fonts and spacing. Use Edit > Paste Special and pick plain text.
Turning on Design Ideas before you test your custom template.
Building one huge deck for a full course. Split it by module so reviews and version history stay manageable.

blocks.text: Accessibility and alt text for course slides

Every image in a course needs alt text, or a learner using a screen reader hears nothing useful. On Mac, right-click the picture and choose Edit Alt Text. Describe what the image shows and why it matters to the lesson. Skip phrases like image of, because the reader already knows it is an image.
Run Review > Check Accessibility on each module before you export it. Reading order matters for screen readers. Put the title first, then the content in the order a learner reads it on screen.
Next steps for an instructional designer on a Mac

items: Open View > Slide Master and fix one layout today, not the whole theme.
Save the master as a PowerPoint Template (.potx) and test it with a sample module.
Write one storyboard in the table format above, then ask a reviewer to read it on a phone.
Check your Microsoft 365 plan for organization templates and Designer access.
Try Lazur for the steps you keep forgetting, then compare notes with your team.

blocks.text: If you also build client decks, the consultant page covers slides, charts and layouts in the same Microsoft 365 tools. The [PowerPoint app page](/apps/powerpoint) explains how Lazur answers questions about slides and finds buttons. When you are ready, [download Lazur](/download) and compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing).
Keep the template small and the storyboard honest. A clean master saves more time than any single shortcut, and it keeps every course looking like it came from one team.

faq.question: Is PowerPoint good enough for instructional design on Mac?
faq.answer: For short modules and storyboards, yes. The iSpring guide says the format can become cumbersome for very long, text-heavy courses. When a course grows, split it into module files and consider a dedicated authoring tool for the final build.

faq.question: Where is the slide master in PowerPoint on Mac?
faq.answer: Go to View > Slide Master. The Slide Master tab opens with the master slide at the top of the thumbnail pane and the layouts listed below it. Edit the layouts there, not on regular slides.

faq.question: Can I use Designer or Design Ideas on Mac?
faq.answer: Designer needs a Microsoft 365 subscription. Microsoft lists PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 for Mac in the feature's Applies To list. Not all custom templates work with Design Suggestions, so test it on your template first.

faq.question: Why does Microsoft's template article show Windows steps?
faq.answer: Microsoft's template page gives Windows steps, and its linked Mac article returned a 404 when checked. Use the Mac menu paths in this guide, then confirm the save format and menu names on your own version.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my slides for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at things, guides you one click at a time, answers out loud and drafts text you can paste or dictate. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Which PowerPoint version should a team standardize on?
faq.answer: Pick one version and write it down. Microsoft's Mac help covers Microsoft 365 for Mac, PowerPoint 2024 for Mac and PowerPoint 2021 for Mac. Steps can differ between them, so a shared guide should name the version.

faq.question: Will the right-click menu change affect my templates?
faq.answer: The change removes Zoom from the slide and thumbnail menus, and it adds Layout and Reset Slide. It rolls out in October 2026 with no admin controls, so tell your team before it arrives. Templates and masters are not affected by the menu itself.
